title: Cold comfort: What China can teach Europe about adaptation – European Council on Foreign Relations
gist: As Chinese air conditioners flood the EU market amid worsening European heatwaves, the author argues Europe's real lesson from China isn't to adapt to trade dependency but to copy China's own refusal to accept fixed comparative advantage — by preserving optionality through diversified suppliers (South Korea, Japan, India, Gulf states) rather than either total dependence on China or an unaffordable 'reverse Deng' subsidy race.

themes.theme: Climate adaptation costs are already here

insights.claim: Europe's summer 2026 heatwaves have forced school closures, disrupted railways, cut nuclear power plant output, been linked to more than 25,000 excess deaths across the continent, and caused wildfires with over €15bn of economic damage.
insights.speaker: Byford Tsang
insights.so_what: Quantifies near-term climate-adaptation cost exposure for European utilities (nuclear output), transport, and public health/insurance sectors.
insights.quote: More than 25,000 excess deaths across Europe have been attributed to extreme heat so far, while wildfires are causing over €15bn of economic damage.

insights.claim: Cooling is becoming essential infrastructure comparable to heating and water, meaning Europe will need a broad portfolio of solutions — air conditioning alongside passive-cooling technologies like evaporative cooling, reflective roofs, building retrofits and stronger building standards — rather than relying on any single import channel.
insights.speaker: Byford Tsang
insights.so_what: Points to a multi-technology cooling infrastructure buildout opportunity beyond just AC unit imports — relevant to building-retrofit and passive-cooling suppliers.

themes.theme: China's AC export boom and Europe's growing dependency

insights.claim: China produces over 80% of the world's air conditioners; Chinese AC exports to the EU rose 43% year-on-year in the first half of 2026, and Chinese brands now hold 41% of the European AC market, up from 27% in 2023.
insights.speaker: Byford Tsang
insights.so_what: Tracks a fast-growing, concentrated import dependency in a climate-adaptation product category — a concrete metric for EU trade-defence and de-risking debates.
insights.quote: China produces over 80% of the world’s air conditioners: exports of Chinese AC units to the EU rose by 43% year on year in the first half of 2026. Chinese brands now account for 41% of the European market, up from 27% in 2023.

insights.claim: Chinese manufacturers' European market gains go beyond price and scale: Midea's PortaSplit portable-split model was specifically engineered to overcome EU building regulations and high installation costs, and Chinese firms were early adopters of climate-friendlier refrigerants that meet strict EU environmental rules.
insights.speaker: Byford Tsang
insights.so_what: Suggests European AC competitors face a genuine product-design and regulatory-adaptation gap, not just a cost disadvantage — a harder competitive problem to solve with tariffs alone.

insights.claim: Chinese state media frame the AC export boom as a 'win-win' born of complementary advantages and portray EU de-risking and trade-defence measures as economically self-defeating; the author calls this a 'fatalistic prescription' for industrial policy from a country that has never accepted its own position in global supply chains as fixed.
insights.speaker: Byford Tsang
insights.so_what: Warns investors and policymakers against taking Beijing's 'accept comparative advantage' messaging at face value, since China itself never follows that logic for its own strategic sectors.
insights.quote: This is a fatalistic prescription for industrial policy from a country that refuses to accept that its position in global supply chains or its existing competitive advantage is fixed.

themes.theme: Lessons from China's own industrial playbook

insights.claim: China's industrial transformation was never passive market adaptation: under 'Made in China' and 'Dual Circulation,' and now a five-year plan emphasising 'self-reliance and controllability,' Beijing deployed large-scale subsidies, preferential state-bank financing, government-guided investment funds, public procurement preference, and joint-venture/localisation/tech-transfer requirements to build globally competitive firms in strategic sectors like robotics, clean tech and aviation.
insights.speaker: Byford Tsang
insights.so_what: Provides a concrete checklist of tools China used that Europe would need to match if it tried a true industrial-policy response — useful baseline for evaluating EU competitiveness proposals.

insights.claim: The author argues Europe should not attempt a 'reverse Deng' — matching the scale of state-directed subsidy and protection China used in the 1990s-2000s — because the EU lacks a centralised state able to direct capital and absorb the commercial losses such a strategy requires; instead the real lesson is to preserve optionality by minimising strategically constraining dependencies and maintaining viable alternative suppliers.
insights.speaker: Byford Tsang
insights.so_what: Argues against an EU industrial-subsidy arms race with China and instead for a supplier-diversification strategy — relevant to how EU competitiveness/de-risking funding should be allocated.
insights.quote: Europeans should preserve their ability to source and scale critical technologies through viable alternatives, ensuring they have options should conditions change

insights.claim: South Korea, the world's second-largest battery manufacturer, holds 78% of installed battery capacity in Europe; Japan has diversified its rare-earth supply through partnerships with Australia, Malaysia and Vietnam; and India doubled its solar-cell manufacturing capacity in the first half of 2026, backed by localisation incentives extending upstream to ingots and polysilicon.
insights.speaker: Byford Tsang
insights.so_what: Names concrete non-China suppliers and current market shares in batteries, rare earths and solar — a starting map for supply-chain diversification investment.

insights.claim: The author proposes Europe build a network of alternative suppliers rather than attempting full domestic production of every critical technology — partnering with Singapore and Gulf states on district cooling, and with South Korea, Japan and India on clean-tech supply chains, using reciprocal public-procurement access, targeted incentives and shared product standards.
insights.speaker: Byford Tsang
insights.so_what: Outlines a concrete diversification blueprint (partner-country list plus policy tools) the EU could pursue instead of costly full re-shoring.

themes.theme: Climate policy as the model for economic security

insights.claim: The author frames 'having options' — adapting to a problem while simultaneously tackling its cause — as the core strategic principle for both climate policy and economic security: just as Europe pursues both adaptation (AC, seawalls) and mitigation (cutting fossil-fuel emissions) for climate change, it should both manage near-term trade dependencies and invest in reducing the underlying vulnerabilities.
insights.speaker: Byford Tsang
insights.so_what: A reusable mental model connecting climate-adaptation logic to economic-security policy — useful framing for how the EU should structure de-risking budgets going forward.

insights.claim: The author warns that adapting to today's trade dependencies in the name of short-term efficiency will leave Europe with fewer strategic options and a larger economic bill later, drawing a direct parallel to the cost of delayed climate action.
insights.speaker: Byford Tsang
insights.so_what: A forward-looking warning against complacency on supply-chain dependency, framed as a cost that compounds the longer it's deferred.
insights.quote: adapting to today’s dependencies in the name of efficiency will leave Europe with fewer options—and come with a larger bill—tomorrow
